title: Breaking the Grid: Distance-Guided Reinforcement Learning in Large Discrete Action Spaces
claim: Our method reaches higher reward and converges faster than competing baselines across structured, irregular, and very large discrete action-space environments.
layout: 2x4 grid of learning curves, shared legend below, ours in red
description: A 2x4 grid of line plots of median reward with shaded IQR bands against training episodes. The top row shows four Maze variants: 5^4 and 17^10 action spaces, each in two settings marked (S) and (I). The bottom row shows Job Shop Scheduling, Joint Replenishment, and two Recommender tasks with action spaces from 343^1 to 343^10. A red curve for the proposed method (DGRL) rises quickly and plateaus at the top in nearly every panel. Baselines are drawn in purple, green, orange, blue, black and brown. Several baselines collapse, stay flat, or show wide shaded variance bands, especially on the larger action spaces. A single legend across the bottom names each method with its underlying algorithm (A2C or DDPG). The eye goes to the red curve first.

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is increasingly applied to large-scale decision-making problems like logistics, scheduling, and recommender systems, but existing algorithms struggle with the curse of dimensionality in such large discrete action spaces. We propose Distance-Guided Reinforcement Learning (DGRL), combining Sampled Dynamic Neighborhoods and Distance-Based Updates to enable efficient RL in problems with up to $10^{36}$ actions. Unlike prior methods, DGRL performs stochastic volumetric exploration and transforms policy optimization into a stable regression task, decoupling gradient variance from action space cardinality. On structured tasks, DGRL provably guarantees local value improvement. DGRL naturally handles action spaces without regular semantic structure and hybrid continuous-discrete action spaces. We demonstrate performance improvements of up to 66% against state-of-the-art benchmarks across regularly and irregularly structured environments, while simultaneously improving convergence speed and computational complexity.
